stories.headline: FED HIKES RATES FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2023, WARSH SIGNALS MORE TO COME
stories.body: The FOMC voted 12-0 to raise the federal funds rate a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00%, its first hike in three years. Chairman Kevin Warsh said "this summer's inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," and 16 of 18 officials penciled in at least one more hike before year-end.
stories.explain: A unanimous vote paired with hawkish dot-plot guidance is a stronger signal than the hike itself, because markets had already priced a 25 bp move at roughly 90%+ odds going in. What wasn't fully priced was Warsh explicitly rejecting the "inflation is cooling" narrative, which is why yields, the dollar, and gold all moved sharply on his press conference rather than on the 2:00 PM statement release.

stories.headline: DOW SHEDS 631 POINTS AS RATE-SENSITIVE STOCKS SLIDE, CHIPS BUCK THE TREND
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.45% to 7,551.81 and the Dow dropped 1.21% to 51,461.90 after Warsh's hawkish remarks, with J.B. Hunt's surprise profit warning also dragging transports lower. The Nasdaq 100 held up better, adding 0.58% to 29,104.35 as an AI-and-semiconductor rally led by AMD, Marvell, and Intel offset the broader selloff.
stories.explain: The Dow and S&P are more exposed to cyclical, rate-sensitive sectors like industrials and financials, which get hit hardest when the discount rate on future cash flows rises unexpectedly. The Nasdaq 100's resilience shows investors are treating this week's chip rally as an idiosyncratic, fundamentals-driven story (AI capex demand) that's strong enough to offset the same higher-rate headwind dragging down the rest of the index.

stories.headline: WTI CRUDE TUMBLES 3.3% ON SURPRISE INVENTORY BUILD DESPITE MIDDLE EAST DISRUPTIONS
stories.body: WTI fell to $102.31 a barrel even as Brent held near $108 on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline outage, after industry data showed a surprise build in U.S. crude inventories. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the Saudi pipeline, which routes 7 million barrels a day away from the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, should resume "within days," though independent analysts see a multi-week repair.
stories.explain: The WTI-Brent split here is a domestic-supply-versus-geopolitical-risk story: a bigger-than-expected U.S. inventory build signals near-term oversupply at home, while Brent stays elevated because it's the benchmark most exposed to the Hormuz/Red Sea routing risk. If Wright's "within days" timeline proves wrong, expect Brent's premium over WTI to widen further as the market re-prices a longer Saudi outage.

stories.headline: GOLD DROPS TO $4,310 AS REAL YIELDS SPIKE ON HAWKISH FED
stories.body: Gold gave back its morning gains within a half hour of the Fed's decision, sliding roughly 1% to $4,310 an ounce as the 10-year yield jumped 21 basis points to 5.01% on Warsh's inflation comments.
stories.explain: Gold carries no coupon, so its opportunity cost rises directly with real (inflation-adjusted) yields — when the 10-year jumps 21 bps in an afternoon and near-term inflation expectations don't move nearly as much, the real yield on Treasuries rises and gold becomes comparatively less attractive to hold. That's why gold sold off even with an active Middle East oil-supply shock in the background, a scenario that would normally support a safe-haven bid.

stories.headline: DOLLAR POSTS BIGGEST ONE-DAY GAIN SINCE JUNE, DXY TOPS 100 FOR FIRST TIME SINCE JULY
stories.body: The DXY jumped 0.61% to 100.28, its highest close since July 31 and biggest single-day gain since mid-June, as traders repriced toward three total Fed hikes through next June following Warsh's remarks.
stories.explain: A hike that comes with a hawkish forward path widens the expected interest-rate differential between the dollar and other major currencies for longer than a single 25 bp move would on its own, which is what pulls capital toward dollar assets. The move also partially offsets today's oil story for U.S. consumers, since a stronger dollar makes dollar-priced Brent crude marginally cheaper in real terms even as the headline barrel price stays elevated.

stories.headline: PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT CLEARS FIRST PROCEDURAL VOTE, 74-24
stories.body: The Senate advanced the Protect College Sports Act in the first of three required procedural votes, with a second vote possible as soon as Thursday and a final vote expected next week. Separately, Indiana landed a 2027 commitment from German 7-footer Felix Kiehlneker, and the NCAA won another court victory keeping several transfer-eligibility cases, including Gonzaga's Javon Bennett, on hold.

stories.headline: KAWHI LEONARD TRADE TO RAPTORS OFFICIALLY COMPLETE AFTER MONTHS-LONG LEAGUE INVESTIGATION
stories.body: The Clippers and Raptors finalized the deal sending Leonard to Toronto for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two unprotected first-round picks, a pick swap, and two second-rounders, after the trade was held up since June 30 while the league investigated Clippers cap-circumvention allegations. Leonard, coming off a 27.9 ppg season, waived a $7.45M trade kicker and is expected to sign an extension in Toronto.

stories.headline: CHIEFS' KENNETH WALKER III RUSHES FOR 173 YARDS IN DEBUT AS KC ROUTS DENVER 31-10
stories.body: Walker III broke a 60-yard touchdown run in his first game in Kansas City as the Chiefs dominated the Broncos on Monday Night Football, while Travis Kelce moved into second place all-time in receiving yards by a tight end. The Chiefs-Broncos game helped tie the Super Bowl-era record for combined points scored in a Week 1 slate.

stories.headline: LSU DEMOLISHES CLEMSON 51-10, PILING PRESSURE ON DABO SWINNEY
stories.body: LSU blew out Clemson 51-10 in one of the most lopsided results of the season's opening weeks, while Michigan survived a controversial finish to escape Western Michigan 13-12. Texas QB Arch Manning, Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith, and Notre Dame QB CJ Carr remain the top names on early Heisman watch lists.

deepDive.title: Why the Dot Plot Moved Markets More Than the Rate Hike Itself
content: Today's Fed decision was almost a non-event by the time it hit the tape — a quarter-point hike to 3.75%-4.00% had been priced at well over 90% odds for weeks. Yet the 10-year yield jumped 21 basis points, the dollar posted its biggest one-day gain since June, and gold gave back its entire morning rally within thirty minutes. The mover wasn't the vote count; it was Chairman Warsh's press conference and the committee's updated Summary of Economic Projections, better known as the dot plot. Understanding why forward guidance can swamp the actual policy action explains almost every market move in today's brief.

The dot plot is a scatter chart where each of the 18 FOMC participants marks their own projection for where the fed funds rate will sit at the end of each of the next several years, plus a longer-run estimate. It says nothing binding — no one votes on the dots, and individual policymakers can and do abandon their own projections within a quarter — but it's the clearest signal the Fed gives about its reaction function, the internal model of how officials will respond to incoming data. Today's dots showed 16 of 18 participants expecting at least one more hike in 2026, with four seeing two. That distribution matters more than today's single hike because it prices an entire path, not one data point.

This is why markets can rally on a rate cut and sell off on a rate hike, or vice versa, depending entirely on guidance: in December 2018, the Fed hiked rates as expected but Chair Powell's press conference described the balance-sheet runoff as being on "autopilot," and the S&P 500 fell nearly 2% that day and kept falling into a near-bear-market by Christmas Eve, purely on the forward-guidance language. Most people conflate "what the Fed did" with "what the Fed said it will do next," but bond and currency markets are pricing machines built on expectations — they had already settled today's hike into yields over the prior weeks, leaving Warsh's hawkish framing as the only genuinely new information of the day.

For a student watching this unfold, the practical lesson is where to look next: the CME FedWatch-style probability of additional 2026 hikes, the pace of core PCE readings between now and the next meeting, and whether Warsh's language holds or softens at the October meeting. If the coming CPI and PCE prints come in soft, expect today's hawkish repricing — the higher 10-year, the stronger dollar, the weaker gold — to partially unwind, since the dot plot is a snapshot of officials' current thinking, not a commitment. The next real test of today's guidance isn't the next Fed meeting; it's the next inflation print.
